In what order should you look?","fact_ids":["sec06-F04"]},"answer":{"text":"Left, then right, then left again.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04"]},"rationale":{"text":"Just before entering an intersection, look left, then right, then left again.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Giving yourself time and space","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-R03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Look far ahead.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-R03"]},{"text":"Follow at a safe distance.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-R03"]},{"text":"Leave room to maneuver.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-R03"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson begins the defensive driving guidelines. Giving yourself time and space to stop is easier if you look far enough ahead, keep enough distance from the car in front, and choose a position in traffic that leaves you options. We will cover the twelve-second look-ahead and how to check it, the two-second minimum following distance and how to count it, why more room is needed at higher speeds, how to keep room to maneuver, and how to look before entering an intersection. These habits cost nothing and prevent many of the most common crashes.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-R03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Looking ahead","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Look at least twelve seconds ahead.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01"]},{"text":"At thirty, a little over a block.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01"]},{"text":"Freeways: twenty to thirty seconds.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Look ahead at least twelve seconds, to the spot your vehicle will reach twelve seconds from now. At thirty miles per hour, that is a little more than one block. To test your look-ahead, pick a fixed object in front of you and count one-thousand-one upward until your front bumper reaches it; if you have not got to one-thousand-twelve, look farther ahead. At freeway speeds, look at least twenty to thirty seconds ahead. Looking far down the road lets you see traffic patterns change and react before you are forced to brake suddenly.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Following distance","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02","sec06-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Two seconds is the minimum.","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02","sec06-F03"]},{"text":"Up to four is recommended.","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02","sec06-F03"]},{"text":"More room at speed and on slick roads.","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02","sec06-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"If you drive forty miles per hour or less, keep at least two seconds behind the vehicle ahead. That is only the minimum, and most driving instructors recommend up to four seconds. To test it, start counting when the rear of the car ahead passes a fixed point such as a sign; reaching that point before one-thousand-two means you are too close. Stopping from fifty-five miles per hour takes almost seven seconds even with perfect brakes and ideal roads, so leave more room at highway speeds and whenever roads are slippery or visibility is poor.","fact_ids":["sec06-F02","sec06-R02","sec06-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Two different counts","fact_ids":["sec06-R01","sec06-R02","sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Twelve: how far ahead you look.","fact_ids":["sec06-R01","sec06-R02","sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]},{"text":"Two: how far behind you follow.","fact_ids":["sec06-R01","sec06-R02","sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]},{"text":"Both use a fixed object.","fact_ids":["sec06-R01","sec06-R02","sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from two counts that sound alike. Both tests use a fixed object and counting one-thousand-one, but they measure different things. The twelve-second count measures how far ahead you are looking: count until your own front bumper reaches the object, and you should reach one-thousand-twelve. The two-second count measures following distance: count from when the car ahead passes the object, and you should reach at least one-thousand-two before you get there. Mixing them up leads to answers like a twelve-second following gap or a two-second look-ahead.","fact_ids":["sec06-R01","sec06-R02","sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check an intersection","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"About to enter an intersection.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-F01"]},{"text":"In what order do you look?","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are about to enter an intersection. In what order should you look, just before you go in? Recall the sequence before reading on. Look left, then right, then left again. Finishing on the left means your last look is at the lane of traffic nearest to you. Combined with looking twelve seconds ahead and keeping a safe following gap, this final check before an intersection is one of the simplest ways to avoid being hit by someone you did not see. Then look twelve seconds ahead again as you go through.","fact_ids":["sec06-F04","sec06-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Space recap","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01","sec06-F02","sec06-R02","sec06-F03","sec06-R03","sec06-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Twelve seconds ahead, more on freeways.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01","sec06-F02","sec06-R02","sec06-F03","sec06-R03","sec06-F04"]},{"text":"Two seconds behind at minimum.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01","sec06-F02","sec06-R02","sec06-F03","sec06-R03","sec06-F04"]},{"text":"Stay between clusters of cars.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01","sec06-F02","sec06-R02","sec06-F03","sec06-R03","sec06-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To review, look at least twelve seconds ahead, about a block at thirty miles per hour, and twenty to thirty seconds on freeways, checking it by counting to a fixed object. Keep at least two seconds behind the car ahead at forty miles per hour or less, up to four is better, and much more at highway speed, since stopping from fifty-five takes almost seven seconds. Keep room to maneuver by adjusting your speed and lane so you sit between clusters of vehicles in the lane with the most options. Before entering an intersection, look left, right and left again.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-R01","sec06-F02","sec06-R02","sec06-F03","sec06-R03","sec06-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec06-u02","module_id":"sec06-m02","objective_ids":["sec06-u02"],"title":{"text":"Phones and police stops","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-F07"]},"why_how":[{"text":"A phone in your hand takes your attention off the road, so Nevada bans most handheld use while driving.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06"]},{"text":"Knowing what to do when police stop you keeps the stop safe and quick for everyone.","fact_ids":["sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]},{"text":"One narrow exception lets you use a handheld phone to report an emergency when stopping would be unsafe.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"A driver's phone buzzes with a text while waiting in slow traffic.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Using a handheld device by hand to read or send messages is prohibited while driving.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06"]},"result":{"text":"The driver leaves the phone alone until parked; reading the text in traffic would break the law.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a quick look at a text is allowed in slow traffic.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06"]},"correction":{"text":"Reading, sending or searching on a handheld device is prohibited while driving, whatever the speed.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Hands-free to talk, hands off to text.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You see a serious crash ahead and stopping right away would be dangerous. May you use your handheld phone to report it?","fact_ids":["sec06-F07"]},"answer":{"text":"Yes.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07"]},"rationale":{"text":"A handheld device may be used to report an emergency when stopping would be inadvisable, impractical or dangerous.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Phones and police","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Phone rules while driving.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F08"]},{"text":"What to do when stopped.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers two situations every driver faces: the phone and the police stop. Nevada limits how you may use a cell phone or other handheld wireless device while driving, with a narrow exception for emergencies. It also gives clear guidance on what to do when you see flashing lights behind you, how to act while the officer approaches, and how to handle a citation you disagree with. Following these steps keeps you within the law and keeps a traffic stop calm and safe for you, your passengers and the officer. Each step has a reason.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Handheld device rules","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Voice calls need a hands-free accessory.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-F07"]},{"text":"No texting, messaging or web searching.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-F07"]},{"text":"Emergency reports are the exception.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Holding a cell phone or other handheld wireless device for a voice call while driving is prohibited unless you use a hands-free accessory. Using a handheld device by hand to text, send or read messages, search the Internet or otherwise communicate without voice is also prohibited while driving. You may use a handheld device to report an emergency when stopping the vehicle would be inadvisable, impractical or dangerous. So talking is allowed only hands-free, texting is never allowed, and the emergency report is the one exception for a handheld phone.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"When police stop you","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pull far out of the traffic lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]},{"text":"Stay inside; interior light on at night.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]},{"text":"Hands visible, no sudden moves.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Moving violations such as speeding, running a light or sign, not signalling or leaving your marked lane are the most common reason police stop a vehicle, and drivers can break a law without knowing it. If police lights flash behind you, pull over as far out of the traffic lane as you can and stay inside the vehicle. At night, switch on the interior light. Keep your hands where the officer can see them, ideally on the steering wheel, avoid sudden movements, and wait to be asked for your license, registration and proof of insurance.","fact_ids":["sec06-R04","sec06-F08","sec06-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Arguing at the roadside","fact_ids":["sec06-R05","sec06-R04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Papers first, explanation second.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05","sec06-R04"]},{"text":"Hand them over without argument.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05","sec06-R04"]},{"text":"Contest a ticket in court.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05","sec06-R04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap. A driver who believes a stop is unfair may want to argue the point right there. The handbook advises against it. Officers usually ask for identification first and explain the stop second, so hand over the requested papers promptly and without argument, then give the officer a chance to explain. If you think the citation was issued wrongly, the proper way to contest it is to request a court hearing, or attend the hearing named in your notice, rather than arguing at the roadside. Presenting the paperwork promptly also speeds up the stop.","fact_ids":["sec06-R05","sec06-R04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the emergency exception","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F05","sec06-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"A serious crash ahead.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F05","sec06-F06"]},{"text":"Stopping now would be dangerous.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F05","sec06-F06"]},{"text":"May you use your phone?","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F05","sec06-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you see a serious crash ahead, and stopping right away would be dangerous. May you use your handheld phone to report it? Decide before reading on. Yes. You may use a handheld device to report an emergency when stopping the vehicle would be inadvisable, impractical or dangerous. That is the only exception for handheld use. Everyday calls still require a hands-free accessory, and texting, reading messages or searching the Internet by hand are prohibited while driving, no matter how slowly you are moving.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F05","sec06-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":35,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Phones and stops recap","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-F07","sec06-R04","sec06-F08","sec06-F09","sec06-R05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Hands-free calls only; no texting.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-F07","sec06-R04","sec06-F08","sec06-F09","sec06-R05"]},{"text":"Emergency reports allowed.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-F07","sec06-R04","sec06-F08","sec06-F09","sec06-R05"]},{"text":"Calm, visible, cooperative at a stop.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-F07","sec06-R04","sec06-F08","sec06-F09","sec06-R05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us sum up. Handheld voice calls need a hands-free accessory, handheld texting, messaging and web use are prohibited while driving, and reporting an emergency is allowed when stopping would be unsafe. Moving violations are the most common reason for a stop. When lights flash behind you, pull far out of traffic, stay inside, turn on the interior light at night, keep your hands visible on the wheel and wait to be asked for your documents. Hand them over without argument, and contest a citation through the court, not at the roadside.","fact_ids":["sec06-F05","sec06-F06","sec06-F07","sec06-R04","sec06-F08","sec06-F09","sec06-R05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec06-u03","module_id":"sec06-m03","objective_ids":["sec06-u03"],"title":{"text":"Roundabouts, signals and turns","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Roundabouts move traffic without signals, but only if every driver yields and picks the right lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11"]},{"text":"Signals and correct lane position tell other drivers what you are about to do, and the law requires them.","fact_ids":["sec06-F13","sec06-F15","sec06-F16"]},{"text":"If your signal lights fail, hand signals let you keep telling other drivers what you plan to do.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"You want to go straight through a two-lane roundabout and must choose a lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-F11"]},"reasoning":{"text":"The left lane is for left turns, U-turns or going straight, and the right lane is for right turns or going straight.","fact_ids":["sec06-F11"]},"result":{"text":"Either lane works for going straight, so you choose one, yield to circulating traffic and signal right as you exit.","fact_ids":["sec06-F11","sec06-F10","sec06-F12"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a right-turn-only lane can be used to drive straight through when traffic is light.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16"]},"correction":{"text":"A lane reserved for right turns may be entered only to turn right, never to drive straight through.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Arm out left, arm up right, arm down slow.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"Your turn signals stop working and you need to turn right. How do you signal by hand?","fact_ids":["sec06-F14"]},"answer":{"text":"Left arm bent upward at about a right angle.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14"]},"rationale":{"text":"The right-turn hand signal is the left arm bent upward; straight out means left, and pointed down with palm back means slowing or stopping.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Turning and circling","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Roundabouts.","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F13"]},{"text":"Signals and hand signals.","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F13"]},{"text":"Turns and lane changes.","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers roundabouts, signalling, turns and lane changes. A roundabout is a circular intersection that controls the right-of-way without traffic signals, and it works only when drivers yield and choose the right lane. Signalling before you turn, change lanes, slow down, stop or park is required by law, not just a courtesy, and hand signals take over when lights fail. We will also look at how to position the car for right and left turns, which lane to enter after turning, and how to change lanes safely. Many crashes happen during turns, so precision matters here.","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Driving a roundabout","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-R06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yield to traffic already circulating.","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-R06"]},{"text":"Traffic moves counterclockwise.","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-R06"]},{"text":"Signal right as you exit.","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-R06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Drivers entering a roundabout must yield to the traffic already circulating in it, and all traffic travels around it counterclockwise. In a two-lane roundabout, use the left lane to turn left, make a U-turn or go straight, and the right lane to turn right or go straight. Inside a roundabout, slow to the speed of the traffic already circulating, and switch on your right turn signal as you exit. Large trucks and trailers may run their rear wheels over the raised truck apron around the center island to manage the tight turn, but cars should stay off the apron.","fact_ids":["sec06-F10","sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-R06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Others in the roundabout","fact_ids":["sec06-R07","sec06-R08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Cyclists may take the lane or walk.","fact_ids":["sec06-R07","sec06-R08"]},{"text":"Pedestrians use the crosswalks.","fact_ids":["sec06-R07","sec06-R08"]},{"text":"Never cross to the central island.","fact_ids":["sec06-R07","sec06-R08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Cyclists who are comfortable in traffic may take the lane in a roundabout, yield when entering, keep to traffic speed and hand-signal when leaving; otherwise they may walk the bike through the crosswalks. Pedestrians at a roundabout must stay in the marked crosswalks and never cross to the central island. They have the right-of-way, but they should still watch for cars. As a driver, expect cyclists riding at traffic speed in your lane, and watch the crosswalks at each entry and exit, where pedestrians cross in front of vehicles entering and leaving the circle.","fact_ids":["sec06-R07","sec06-R08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Signals and hand signals","fact_ids":["sec06-F13","sec06-F15","sec06-F14"]},"lines":[{"text":"Signalling is the law.","fact_ids":["sec06-F13","sec06-F15","sec06-F14"]},{"text":"City: one hundred feet ahead.","fact_ids":["sec06-F13","sec06-F15","sec06-F14"]},{"text":"Open highway: three hundred feet.","fact_ids":["sec06-F13","sec06-F15","sec06-F14"]}],"narration":{"text":"Signalling before you turn, change lanes, slow down, stop or park is required by law. On city streets, turn your signal on no less than one hundred feet, about ten car lengths, before the turn; on open highways, make it three hundred feet, about thirty car lengths. If your signals fail, use hand signals: a left arm held straight out means a left turn, a left arm bent upward at about a right angle means a right turn, and a left arm pointed down with the palm facing back means slowing or stopping. Every hand signal uses the left arm.","fact_ids":["sec06-F13","sec06-F15","sec06-F14"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Right and left turns","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R09","sec06-F17","sec06-R10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Right: far right lane or right-turn lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R09","sec06-F17","sec06-R10"]},{"text":"Left: wheels straight until turning.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R09","sec06-F17","sec06-R10"]},{"text":"Enter the nearest correct lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R09","sec06-F17","sec06-R10"]}],"narration":{"text":"For a right turn, be in the far right travel lane or a lane marked for right turns. After the turn, enter the right-hand lane of the new road or the lane marked for the turn, and change lanes only after signalling once you are well clear of the intersection. For a left turn, keep the wheels pointed straight until you actually start turning, and on a two-way road turn from the lane just right of the center line into the nearest lane going your way. Many crashes come from turns, so watch for pedestrians and cyclists and look once more in each direction before turning.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-R09","sec06-F17","sec06-R10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s6","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Two kinds of right lanes","fact_ids":["sec06-F11","sec06-F16"]},"lines":[{"text":"Roundabout right lane: right or straight.","fact_ids":["sec06-F11","sec06-F16"]},{"text":"Right-turn-only lane: right only.","fact_ids":["sec06-F11","sec06-F16"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap with two right lanes. In a two-lane roundabout, the right lane may be used to turn right or to go straight. At an ordinary intersection, a lane reserved for right turns may be entered only to turn right, never to drive straight through. So the word right lane does not always mean the same thing. When a question describes a roundabout, either lane can take you straight. When it describes a marked right-turn-only lane at a regular intersection, going straight from that lane is not allowed, no matter how light the traffic is or how clear the way ahead looks.","fact_ids":["sec06-F11","sec06-F16"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check a hand signal","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Your signals have failed.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-F15"]},{"text":"You need to turn right.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: your turn signals stop working, and you need to turn right. How do you signal by hand? Picture the arm position before reading on. Extend your left arm with the elbow bent upward at about a right angle. That is the right-turn signal.
